title: Bea and Nori's Rocket Rescue
markdown:
Once upon a time, in a town buzzing with model rockets, lived Bea Swift. Her hands were often dusty, her eyes sharp, her mind whirling faster than any soldering iron. Her workshop smelled of oil and solder and crackled as she polished her rocket, Comet Chaser. Her best friend was Nori, a robot with wonderfully flexible noodle arms, whose official job was sorting nuts and bolts and whose true purpose was friendship. Bea’s secret dream was to win the prestigious Lunar Launch Model Rocket Competition.

Every day they headed to the dusty field behind the workshop, a wide-open space where wind whispered through tall grass. Bea set up Comet Chaser. Nori stood by, polished sensors like dewdrops. “Ten more degrees up, Nori.” Nori clicked and whirred, adjusting the launchpad with uncanny precision. Small rockets arced into the sky, faint white trails. Bea kept a logbook of every flight.

Until one day the air thickened with confusion. The Lunar Launch competition had begun. The first rocket ignited, veered sharply left, wobbled, and landed in the grass. Then another, and another. Every launcher, including Bea’s, tilted the same peculiar way, as if a mischievous hand had nudged them. A collective gasp.

Bea’s Comet Chaser, despite her calculations, flew in a dizzying circle and landed with a soft thump in Farmer McGregor’s prize pumpkin patch. The farmer let out a bellow that made Bea’s ears ring. The competition screeched to a halt. Bewildered contestants scratched heads. Disgruntled farmers surveyed flattened pumpkins. Bea, with Nori’s steady presence, felt a chill. Not bad luck. Something peculiar.

“This is illogical,” Nori hummed. “The probability of simultaneous malfunction is infinitesimally small. It suggests external influence.”

Because of that, Bea’s sharp eyes scanned the launch area. All launchpads were metal. The tilt was always toward the south. “It’s like someone wanted them to tilt that way. But why?” Her gaze landed on the control booth, where Mr. Grumbles, the competition official, sat agitated, glancing furtively, fingers drumming a nervous beat. Whirs, taps, fidgeting: her mind began to click.

Because of that they began a quiet investigation. While others argued, Bea examined her launchpad. No signs of tampering. Nori extended a sensor arm toward the power conduit. “Energy fluctuations detected. Unusual rhythmic pulsing. Synchronized with Mr. Grumbles’s tapping.” Bea’s mind raced. “Like a signal?” Mr. Grumbles was hiding a small dark object beneath his desk, movements clumsy.

Mr. Grumbles harbored a secret resentment. His ambitious rocket designs had been dismissed. He’d decided the competition would descend into chaos, proving his brilliance another way. He’d developed a sophisticated electromagnetic coil to emit a precise magnetic pulse.

Until finally, with Nori decoding the strange energy patterns, they found a cleverly disguised coil hidden beneath the main launch platform, wires snaking to Mr. Grumbles’s console, humming a low electric thrum. Burnt-sugar air. The next rocket’s countdown blinked. Bea scrambled toward the control booth, risking disqualification. Nori darted forward with surprising speed and snatched the remote-controlled emitter from under the desk just as Mr. Grumbles’s hand reached for it. A collective gasp. Bea, hand steady, found the main power switch for the hidden coil and flipped it off. The hum ceased. Cheers erupted.

Ever since then, rockets at the Lunar Launch soar straight. Bea and Nori are known less for a trophy than for a logbook that still records every degree, and for noodle arms that can snatch a cheat before a countdown hits zero.
characters: Bea (a tinker's daughter), Nori (a noodle-limbed robot)
